title: AI document processing: how accurate is it on financial documents?
description: We benchmarked AI tools on 30 fund reports, with answers locked in advance. Which ones made no mistakes, what each costs per page, and three ways to build it.
summary: Start with the document your team re-keys most, where a wrong number costs money; AI can read it into fields your systems use. Reading itself costs cents; the staff time around it is the real cost[^7][^1]. AI does the reading part, but wrong fields on your own files are the risk, so we built a benchmark that measures them[^20][^7].
verdict: Pick the document your team re-keys most, where a wrong number costs money. Two models from different vendors read it; a person settles only their disagreements[^15][^16].
AI reading costs cents per report[^7]. The $6.00 median to process an invoice is all-in cost, so measure staff minutes and errors per file, not just reading cost[^1].
The two best models made zero mistakes on our 30 fund reports, not your files[^7]. Thirty reports still allow a true error rate of up to about 1 in 10[^19].
The two models disagreed on about 1 fact in 4 (66 of 270); your team settles those and keeps the final say[^7].
First step: benchmark two models on 50 files from one team's queue. Even vendors advise judging tools on your own documents[^20].

pickElse: You process thousands of standard invoices or receipts a day. A cloud prebuilt parser (a ready-made reader for standard forms) costs about $10 per 1,000 pages and handles the volume[^2][^4][^3].

Your files cannot leave your network: run open-source Docling (free for business use)[^6] or a local model. Expect more wrong values: in our first round the two local models made 8 each, where Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 made none[^7].
You only need searchable text, not fields: basic OCR is about $1.50 per 1,000 pages at all three big clouds[^2][^3][^4].

ownData.title: Which AI made the fewest mistakes on 30 fund reports?
ownData.intro: FinExtractBench is our own benchmark of 30 public private-fund reports, 781 pages in all[^7]. We wrote every correct answer by hand and sealed it, meaning locked, before any tool ran[^7]. Each tool read each raw PDF once; a mistake is a wrong value or a value the report never states.
rows: Gemini 4 Carbon (Google; a weaker model, for comparison)
ownData.note: Limits: one person wrote the answers, and the reports are digital, in English and 56 pages at most[^7]. Zero mistakes in 30 reports still allows a true rate of up to about 1 report in 10[^19]. Re-run on 10 reports as scanned page images, both tools still made 0 mistakes[^7].

example.input: A 57-page quarterly report from a private equity fund, as a PDF.
example.output: Money committed (commitment), money paid in (paid-in capital), money paid back out (distributions), and what the fund is worth today (NAV, net asset value). Each fact comes with its page number and the exact words it came from. Any fact the two models disagree on is flagged.

recipes.cost: About $0.27 per report for two top models in our locked-answer round[^7]. The two models disagreed on 66 of 270 facts across all 30 reports, about 1 in 4, and a person settled each[^7].

howToTest: Record today's baseline first: staff minutes per file, and errors that reach the systems and reports downstream.
Pick 50 real files, including your worst scans and longest reports, plus facts some files never state, to catch invented answers. Even vendors advise benchmarking on your own documents[^20].
Write the right answer for every fact before any AI reads the files, and lock it, so the AI's output cannot sway it.
Require each answer to name its page and quote the exact words, and have code check that the quote is there.
Count wrong answers apart from blanks. A blank goes to a person; a wrong number can slip through.
Report minutes per file, wrong fields reaching downstream systems and cost per file, before and after. Run the winner again on new files before you go live.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy a prebuilt parser or an accounts payable tool when your files are standard invoices, receipts or IDs. The big clouds' prebuilt models already cover those[^2][^4]. Buying fits best when you mainly need volume and an audit trail.
buyVsBuild.build: Build on frontier models (the newest, most capable ones) when your files are unique to your business and a wrong number is expensive. The build is a prompt, a fact list, a checker and a review queue where your team settles about 2 facts per report[^7]. If files must stay in-house, run open-source Docling[^6] or a local model; in our benchmark, local models made more wrong values[^7].

watchOuts: Vendor accuracy numbers mostly come from the vendor's own benchmark runs[^20], and public answer keys have errors too[^18]. Even on our locked-answer set, when the AI and our key differed, the AI was right in 22 of 57 cases, so check your key[^7].
A model that writes a plausible wrong number is worse than one that leaves the field blank[^17]. Score them separately.
Two tables on one page with similar labels fooled 7 of 10 tools in our hard round[^7]. Check the facts that sit near look-alikes.
Prices and model versions change: Mistral lists OCR 3 at $2 and OCR 4.1 at $4 per 1,000 pages[^8]. Re-run your benchmark when either changes, and keep the files and answers so the re-run is cheap.
Read the vendor's data terms. Datalab's rate card shows prices with a 25% discount that assumes you let it train on your data[^12].
Plan reviewer time: in our benchmark, about 1 fact in 4 (66 of 270) went to a person[^7]. Multiply by the facts you pull each month to size the workload.

sources.name: Xiong et al., Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (2023)
sources.what: Finds that language models tend to be overconfident when they state their own confidence.

sources.name: Cohen et al., LM vs LM (EMNLP 2023)
sources.what: Having a second model question the first catches factual errors better than earlier methods, often by a large gap.

sources.name: Manakul et al., SelfCheckGPT (EMNLP 2023)
sources.what: Facts that disagree across several answers to the same question are likely invented; consistent facts are likely true.

sources.name: OpenAI, Why language models hallucinate (2025)
sources.what: Argues errors are worse than abstentions and evaluations should penalise confident errors more than uncertainty.

sources.name: Northcutt et al., Pervasive label errors in test sets (2021)
sources.what: Finds at least 3.3% wrong answers on average across 10 widely used benchmark answer keys.

sources.name: Newman, JAMA 1995, interpreting small numerators
sources.what: With zero events in N trials, the upper 95% confidence limit for the true rate is about 3/N.

rules.name: EU AI Act, Annex III
rules.what: Reading documents is not a high-risk use on its own. It becomes part of one when the facts feed credit scoring of people or life and health insurance pricing[^21]. Then logging and human oversight apply[^22][^23], from 2 December 2027[^24][^25].

rules.name: Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9
rules.what: If extracted facts feed a US credit decision, a decline still needs specific reasons[^26], even when an algorithm made it[^27]. A wrongly read fact becomes a wrong reason, so keep the page and quote behind every fact.

rules.name: NYDFS Circular Letter No. 7
rules.what: New York insurers that use AI in underwriting and pricing stay responsible for vendor tools[^28]. Where available, their vendor contracts should give them audit rights[^28].
